segments.say: Lesson 8. Replication, Sharding & Consistent Hashing. Leader-follower, multi-leader, sharding strategies, hot spots, and why consistent hashing minimizes reshuffling.

Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines (for reads and backup). Sharding splits different data across machines (for size and write load). Consistent hashing decides which machine owns which data. Here is an analogy. Replication: photocopies of the same phone book in every branch office. Sharding: splitting the phone book into A–H, I–P and Q–Z volumes kept in different offices.

Why does this matter? How every large system scales its data layer. A few key words. Leader / follower: Writes go to the leader; followers copy it. Replication lag: Followers being slightly behind. Shard: One horizontal slice of the data. Shard key: The field that decides a row's shard. Consistent hashing: Placement that moves little data when servers change.
Replication: leader leads to followers. All writes go to the leader (primary).
The leader streams changes (W A L / binlog) to followers. Async is fast but followers can lag; sync is safe but slower.
Reads scale out across followers. Watch replication lag: a user may not see their own update ("read-your-writes" issue). Route their own reads to the leader briefly.
Leader dies leads to failover: promote a follower. Risk: async replication can lose the last writes, and a split brain if two nodes both think they're leader.
Consistent hashing ring. Naive sharding: server equals hash(key) % N. Add 1 server (N leads to N+1) and almost every key moves, causing a cache wipe or massive data migration.
Consistent hashing: put servers on a ring (hash of server I D leads to position 0. 2 cubed²).
Each key is hashed onto the ring too and belongs to the first server clockwise.
"cart:9" and "img:3" both walk clockwise to Server A.
Add Server D: only keys between C and D (here "cart:9") move to D. About 1/N of keys move, not all of them.
Virtual nodes: each server appears at many ring points to even out the load. Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, C D Ns and distributed caches.

Replication types. Leader-follower: simple, read scaling, failover. The most common. Multi-leader: writes in several regions. Needs conflict resolution (last-write-wins, C R D Ts). Leaderless (Dynamo-style): write to W replicas, read from R, with W plus R greater than N for overlap. Tunable consistency.

Sharding (partitioning) strategies. Range-based: by ranges like user id 1–1M. Supports range scans; risk of hot ranges (recent timestamps). Hash-based: even spread, but range queries hit every shard. Directory / lookup: a service maps key leads to shard. Flexible, but it's an extra hop and a dependency. Geo-based: by region, for data residency.

Sharding pain points. Shard key choice is everything: high cardinality, evenly spread, matches query patterns. Hot spots / celebrity problem: one huge key. Split it with key salting. Cross-shard joins and transactions become hard (scatter-gather, 2PC, sagas). Rebalancing as data grows, which is where consistent hashing helps.

Say it in the interview. "First I'd scale reads with replicas and handle lag via read-your-writes routing. When write volume or data size exceeds one primary, I'd shard on a high-cardinality key that matches the main access pattern, for example user id, using consistent hashing with virtual nodes so adding capacity moves only about 1/N of the data. I'd call out hot keys and cross-shard queries explicitly.".

Let's compare. Range: range scans, simple, hot spots on sequential keys. Hash (mod N): even spread, re-shuffle everything on resize. Consistent hash: ~1/N keys move on resize, more complex; needs vnodes for balance. Directory: flexible placement, lookup service equals dependency.

Replication. Synchronous: higher, no data loss on failover, slowest replica limits writes. Asynchronous: low, may lose recent writes, replication lag. Semi-sync: medium, greater than or equal to 1 replica confirmed, common compromise.

A likely interview question: Explain consistent hashing. A strong answer: Servers and keys are hashed onto a ring, and a key belongs to the next server clockwise. Adding or removing a server only moves the keys in its arc (~1/N). Virtual nodes balance the load.
That's it for Replication, Sharding & Consistent Hashing. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
